tellings.quote: Shortly after the Echo event, a second large-scale, UFO-related ICBM shutdown incident occurred at another of Malmstrom's missile flights, Oscar, according to former Capt. Robert Salas and now-retired Col. Frederick Meiwald, who were the launch officers on duty when it happened.

A short time later, the guard called again and screamed into the phone that a large, glowing, orange-colored, oval-shaped object had suddenly appeared and was silently hovering over the Oscar Launch Control Facility.

Salas quickly woke then-Capt. Meiwald, who was on his rest break, but before he could tell him about the phone calls with the topside guard, they were both shocked to see multiple warning lights indicating the missiles were dropping off alert status—they were malfunctioning.

During a tape-recorded telephone conversation in August 1996, Meiwald, by then a retired colonel, told Salas that shortly after the missiles failed—he remembered six-to-eight, whereas Salas recalls all ten going offline—a two-man security team had been ordered into the field in response to an intrusion alarm at one of the silos.

related.note: The Wall Street Journal explains the same 1967 Malmstrom missile shutdown as an EMP rather than a UFO, a competing core claim about the same event.

plain: On March 24, 1967, according to a former Air Force launch officer named Robert Salas, the nuclear missiles under his watch at Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana shut down one after another while guards reported a glowing object above the site. Salas tells Michels firsthand that he was underground in the Oscar Flight launch control centre, the bunker that could fire a group of ten missiles. Guards on the surface had phoned about strange lights making odd moves, then a horn went off and the first missile "went from green to red", meaning it could no longer be launched. A man named Bob Jameson describes the control wall the same way: "All 10 missiles were off alert. All 10. Whole flight was off alert. All red." If true, something in the sky was able to switch off American nuclear weapons. The researcher Robert Hastings wrote the account down in "The Echo and Oscar Flight Incidents", published in 2012. There, a guard "screamed into the phone that a large, glowing, orange-colored, oval-shaped object" was "silently hovering over the Oscar Launch Control Facility". So the object is orange in his telling, where Michels says red. Hastings also writes that Salas's fellow officer Frederick Meiwald "remembered six-to-eight" missiles failing, "whereas Salas recalls all ten", and Michels himself once says nine of ten. Michels comes back to the case again and again. Karl Nell, a guest speaking from an official background, mentions missiles taken offline at Malmstrom in the 1960s. The filmmaker James Fox and a guest named Kevin Knuth repeat Salas's account, Knuth from a 2010 press conference where Hastings presented six Air Force witnesses. Another guest, Dan Sheehan, says the base commander, Arie Arnoldson, filed a UFO report with NORAD, the joint US and Canadian air defence command.

discussion.by: The Echo and Oscar Flight Incidents
discussion.text: In The Echo and Oscar Flight Incidents (2012), Hastings, telling Salas's account, writes that the guard reported "a large, glowing, orange-colored, oval-shaped object" "silently hovering over the Oscar Launch Control Facility", and that of the missiles that went off alert Meiwald "remembered six-to-eight, whereas Salas recalls all ten going offline". The object is orange in this telling where the tellers say red, and the whole flight of ten is Salas's recollection, which his commander's differs from.
